claim: Older adults' attitudes toward treatment, including perceived stigma or ageism, may discourage them from actively seeking help for mental illness.

claim: Most emphasis has been placed on the importance of biological changes in late-life depression.

claim: There are few theories on psychocognitive etiology of late-life depression.

claim: Emotionally healthy aging has been linked to successful neurocognitive and psychological adaptation to age-related limitations.
source: Important insights into the cognitive-emotional development of LLD may be provided by research on successful aging, which has linked emotionally healthy aging to successful neurocognitive and psychological adaptation to age-related limitations (Carstensen, 2006; Park and Reuter-Lorenz, 2009; Brassen et al., 2012; Mather, 2016; Heckhausen et al., 2019).

claim: Limitations in physical, cognitive, and socioeconomic functioning as well as time perspective become increasingly evident from midlife onward.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Carstensen, 2006; English and Carstensen, 2014; and Heckhausen et al., 2019.

claim: Midlife is a pivotal phase in the life course of well-being.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lachman et al., 2015.

claim: First longitudinal studies support the predictive value of midlife functioning for mood state and depression later in life.
source: Accordingly, first longitudinal studies support the predictive value of midlife functioning for mood state and depression later in life (Dennerstein et al., 2004; Lachman et al., 2015; Campbell et al., 2020).

claim: Some individuals who develop depression at older ages may not have been able to successfully use self-regulatory adaptation strategies at earlier ages.

claim: There is considerable heterogeneity in late-life depression with respect to neuroanatomical, cognitive, clinical, and genetic profiles.

claim: Late-onset depression differs from early-onset depression by an illness onset not before the age of 60.

evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a definition, drawing on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Late-life depression has been associated with the absence of a family history of affective disorders.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fiske et al., 2009 and Naismith et al., 2012.

claim: Some late-life depression subgroups are likely to arise in midlife.

claim: Some late-life depression subgroups are associated with cognitive deficits that may pave the way for clinical symptoms later in life.

claim: The most striking neurobiological feature of late-life depression is the disruption of fronto-subcortical structure.

claim: Disrupted networks in late-life depression include the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, ventromedial PFC, anterior cingulate cortex, basal ganglia, amygdala, and hippocampus.
source: Reported networks include the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), ventromedial PFC (vmPFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), basal ganglia (caudatus, putamen), amygdala, and hippocampus (for comprehensive reviews, see Naismith et al., 2012; Kim and Han, 2021).

claim: The most consistent pattern of decline in late-life depression is located in the anterior cingulate cortex and medial prefrontal cortex compared to age-matched healthy controls.
source: A recently published ALE (activation likelihood estimation) meta-analysis of 17 structural imaging studies with LLD patients reveals the most consistent pattern of decline to be located in the ACC and medial prefrontal cortex compared to age-matched healthy controls.
evidence: The claim is based on a meta-analysis of 17 structural imaging studies, representing aggregated data.

claim: Late-onset late-life depression involves frontoparietal control, dorsal attention, and visual networks.
source: The authors also applied a novel coordinate-based network mapping approach that additionally showed the involvement of frontoparietal control, dorsal attention, and visual networks, particularly in late-onset LLD (Zhukovsky et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhukovsky et al., 2021, which used a novel network mapping approach.

claim: Etiological factors for fronto-subcortical disruptions in late-life depression include vascular mechanisms, inflammation, neuroimmune regulatory dysfunction, neurodegenerative changes, and amyloid accumulation.
source: Several, partially overlapping etiological factors for these disruptions have been discussed, including vascular mechanisms, inflammation, neuroimmune regulatory dysfunction, neurodegenerative changes, and amyloid accumulation (for recent reviews, see Alexopoulos, 2019; Jellinger, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent reviews by Alexopoulos, 2019 and Jellinger, 2022.

claim: White matter lesions are a highly consistent finding in late-life depression.
source: Another highly consistent finding in LLD is the observation of white matter lesions (WMLs), which are recognizable as hyperintense on T2-weighted images and which are predominantly caused by ischemic changes in small vessels (van Agtmaal et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to van Agtmaal et al., 2017.

claim: White matter lesions are predominantly caused by ischemic changes in small vessels.

claim: The vascular depression hypothesis posits that cerebrovascular disease predisposes and/or maintains depression in later life.
source: The observation of WMLs together with common vascular risk factors and cerebrovascular disease (Geraets et al., 2022) have led to the 'vascular depression' hypothesis (Alexopoulos et al., 1997), which posits that cerebrovascular disease predisposes and/or maintains depression in later life.

claim: White matter lesions are mainly localized in subcortical structures and their frontal projections such as the cingulum bundle.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Taylor et al., 2003.

claim: White matter lesion burden is related to reduced cognitive control ability in nondepressed older individuals.

claim: White matter lesion burden in late-life depression is associated with an elevated BOLD response in the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex during an affective-reactivity task.

claim: White matter lesions predict incident depression over time.
source: WMLs predict incident depression over time (van Sloten et al., 2015), and can occur as early as the mid-40s (Moura et al., 2019), and thus can be considered as a strong risk and vulnerability factor for LLD.

claim: White matter lesions can occur as early as the mid-40s.
source: WMLs predict incident depression over time (van Sloten et al., 2015), and can occur as early as the mid-40s (Moura et al., 2019), and thus can be considered as a strong risk and vulnerability factor for LLD.

claim: White matter lesions can be considered as a strong risk and vulnerability factor for late-life depression.
source: WMLs predict incident depression over time (van Sloten et al., 2015), and can occur as early as the mid-40s (Moura et al., 2019), and thus can be considered as a strong risk and vulnerability factor for LLD.

claim: Patients with late-life depression often show severe deficits in executive functions such as cognitive flexibility, planning, response-inhibition or set-shifting.
source: Consistent with structural alterations of networks mediating cognitive control, (Tadayonnejad et al., 2014; Zhukovsky et al., 2021), patients with LLD often show severe deficits in executive functions such as cognitive flexibility, planning, response-inhibition or set-shifting (Herrmann et al., 2007; Naismith et al., 2012), which led to the conceptualization of the 'depression executive dysfunction syndrome' (Alexopoulos, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Herrmann et al., 2007 and Naismith et al., 2012.

claim: Cognitive deficits in late-life depression include impairments in processing speed as well as in learning and memory.

claim: Cognitive deficits in late-life depression are associated with a problematic prognostic and clinical perspective.

claim: Surprisingly few studies have focused specifically on emotional processing or regulation in late-life depression.

claim: Behavioral findings in late-life depression suggest a cognitive bias toward negativity.

claim: Patients with late-life depression show heightened behavioral and autonomic regret responsiveness when being confronted with missed opportunities in a sequential risk-taking task compared to emotionally healthy older adults.

claim: Emotionally healthy older adults show reduced regret responsiveness compared to late-life depression patients and healthy young adults.

claim: Reduced regret responsiveness in emotionally healthy older adults is associated with increased ventromedial prefrontal cortex engagement.

claim: Increased ventromedial prefrontal cortex engagement may help healthy older adults to overcome regretful thoughts.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shiota and Levenson, 2009.

claim: The shift away from explicit, cognitively demanding, toward less costly, attentional, and mainly implicit emotion regulation probably results from reduced cognitive capacity.
source: This shift away from explicit, cognitively demanding, toward less costly, attentional, and mainly implicit (see below) emotion regulation probably results from reduced cognitive capacity (Opitz et al., 2012) and may reflect successful adaptation in terms of SOC (Urry and Gross, 2010).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the shift in emotion regulation strategies, supported by citations to Opitz et al., 2012 and Urry and Gross, 2010.

claim: The shift in emotion regulation may reflect successful adaptation in terms of selection, optimization, and compensation.
source: This shift away from explicit, cognitively demanding, toward less costly, attentional, and mainly implicit (see below) emotion regulation probably results from reduced cognitive capacity (Opitz et al., 2012) and may reflect successful adaptation in terms of SOC (Urry and Gross, 2010).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the shift in emotion regulation strategies, supported by a citation to Urry and Gross, 2010.

claim: Age-effects on emotion regulation have not been consistently observed.
source: It should be noted that age-effects on emotion regulation have not been consistently observed, with some studies reporting no age differences or even suggesting age-similarity in emotion regulation (e.g. Eldesouky and English, 2018; Livingstone and Isaacowitz, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Eldesouky and English, 2018 and Livingstone and Isaacowitz, 2019.

claim: Previous evidence points toward differences in effectiveness and frequency of use of certain emotion regulation strategies in young and older adults.
source: However, previous evidence points toward differences in effectiveness and frequency of use of certain strategies in young and older adults (e.g. Scheibe and Blanchard-Fields, 2009; Shiota and Levenson, 2009), which may be related to age-associated neural changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Scheibe and Blanchard-Fields, 2009 and Shiota and Levenson, 2009.

claim: Older adults' brains may automatically engage in behavior leading to positive emotions through action-value signaling from ventromedial prefrontal cortex/ventral anterior cingulate cortex promoting such behavior.
source: In a similar vein, a recent review suggests that older adults' brains may automatically engage in behavior leading to positive emotions through action-value signaling from vmPFC/ventral ACC promoting such behavior (Isaacowitz, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Isaacowitz, 2022.

claim: Neuroimaging findings on emotion regulation in successful aging indicate a key role of the ventromedial prefrontal cortex/anterior cingulate cortex.
source: Neuroimaging findings on emotion regulation in successful aging indicate a key role of the vmPFC/ACC.
evidence: The claim is stated as a summary of neuroimaging findings.

claim: The strength of ventromedial prefrontal cortex-amygdala coupling at rest predicts the occurrence of a positivity bias in memory.
source: For example, the strength of vmPFC-amygdala coupling at rest predicts the occurrence of a positivity bias in memory (Sakaki et al., 2013), there is an increased ACC/vmPFC activity during selectively focusing on positive information (Leclerc and Kensinger, 2008; Brassen et al., 2011), and activity in the ACC underlying an attentional PE is directly related to emotional well-being in older age (Brassen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sakaki et al., 2013.

claim: There is increased anterior cingulate cortex/ventromedial prefrontal cortex activity during selectively focusing on positive information.
source: For example, the strength of vmPFC-amygdala coupling at rest predicts the occurrence of a positivity bias in memory (Sakaki et al., 2013), there is an increased ACC/vmPFC activity during selectively focusing on positive information (Leclerc and Kensinger, 2008; Brassen et al., 2011), and activity in the ACC underlying an attentional PE is directly related to emotional well-being in older age (Brassen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Leclerc and Kensinger, 2008 and Brassen et al., 2011.

claim: Activity in the anterior cingulate cortex underlying an attentional positivity effect is directly related to emotional well-being in older age.
source: For example, the strength of vmPFC-amygdala coupling at rest predicts the occurrence of a positivity bias in memory (Sakaki et al., 2013), there is an increased ACC/vmPFC activity during selectively focusing on positive information (Leclerc and Kensinger, 2008; Brassen et al., 2011), and activity in the ACC underlying an attentional PE is directly related to emotional well-being in older age (Brassen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brassen et al., 2011.

claim: Increased activation in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex in response to negative information is associated with enhanced striatal signaling.
source: In addition, increased activation in the vmPFC in response to negative information is associated with enhanced striatal (Brassen et al., 2012) and reduced amygdala signaling (Corbett et al., 2020), underlining the critical role of the medial PFC in modulating emotion processing in healthy aging.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brassen et al., 2012.

claim: Increased activation in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex in response to negative information is associated with reduced amygdala signaling.
source: In addition, increased activation in the vmPFC in response to negative information is associated with enhanced striatal (Brassen et al., 2012) and reduced amygdala signaling (Corbett et al., 2020), underlining the critical role of the medial PFC in modulating emotion processing in healthy aging.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Corbett et al., 2020.

claim: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex plays a critical role in modulating emotion processing in healthy aging.
source: In addition, increased activation in the vmPFC in response to negative information is associated with enhanced striatal (Brassen et al., 2012) and reduced amygdala signaling (Corbett et al., 2020), underlining the critical role of the medial PFC in modulating emotion processing in healthy aging.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the associations between vmPFC activation and emotion processing, supported by citations to Brassen et al., 2012 and Corbett et al., 2020.

claim: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex integrates information about current context, goals, motivational states, and learning history to compute and update the subjective value of stimuli and orchestrate appropriate responses to them.
source: The key role of the vmPFC in emotion regulation is based on its unique position to integrate information about current context, goals, motivational states, and learning history to compute and update the subjective value of stimuli and orchestrate appropriate responses to them (Roy et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Roy et al., 2012.

claim: Information about the relevance of stimuli to affective goals is provided mainly by subcortical regions such as the amygdala and the ventral striatum.
source: Information about the relevance of stimuli to affective goals is provided mainly by subcortical regions such as the amygdala and the ventral striatum (Haber and Knutson, 2010), whereas current goals can be represented by more lateral prefrontal regions (Lapate et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Haber and Knutson, 2010.

claim: Current goals can be represented by more lateral prefrontal regions.
source: Information about the relevance of stimuli to affective goals is provided mainly by subcortical regions such as the amygdala and the ventral striatum (Haber and Knutson, 2010), whereas current goals can be represented by more lateral prefrontal regions (Lapate et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lapate et al., 2022.

claim: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex functionally compensates for the decline of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in healthy aging.
source: It has been speculated that the vmPFC functionally compensates for the decline of the dlPFC in healthy aging (Mather, 2016).
evidence: The claim is stated as speculation, supported by a citation to Mather, 2016.

claim: Lateral prefrontal brain regions typically undergo strong age-related decline.
source: Indeed, whereas lateral prefrontal brain regions typically undergo strong age-related decline, the function and structure of the vmPFC remains relatively well preserved across the lifespan (Fjell et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fjell et al., 2009.

claim: The function and structure of the ventromedial prefrontal cortex remains relatively well preserved across the lifespan.
source: Indeed, whereas lateral prefrontal brain regions typically undergo strong age-related decline, the function and structure of the vmPFC remains relatively well preserved across the lifespan (Fjell et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fjell et al., 2009.

claim: Increased activity of the ventromedial prefrontal cortex in response to negative stimuli correlates with lower lateral prefrontal cortex function and structure in healthy older adults.
source: Direct support for this idea is provided by findings that increased activity of the vmPFC in response to negative stimuli correlates with lower lateral PFC function and structure in healthy older adults (van Reekum et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to van Reekum et al., 2018.

claim: Pronounced ventromedial prefrontal cortex engagement reflects a shift toward implicit emotion regulation in healthy aging.
source: It has further been speculated that pronounced vmPFC engagement reflects a shift toward implicit emotion regulation in healthy aging (Suri and Gross, 2012).
evidence: The claim is stated as speculation, supported by a citation to Suri and Gross, 2012.

claim: Most studies demonstrating a positivity effect have not provided explicit instructions for regulating emotions.
source: Indeed, most studies demonstrating a PE have not provided explicit instructions for regulating emotions and most findings could be attributed to an attentional bias (Mather and Carstensen, 2003; Isaacowitz et al., 2008; Brassen et al., 2011; Brassen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mather and Carstensen, 2003; Isaacowitz et al., 2008; Brassen et al., 2011; and Brassen et al., 2012.

claim: Most positivity effect findings could be attributed to an attentional bias.
source: Indeed, most studies demonstrating a PE have not provided explicit instructions for regulating emotions and most findings could be attributed to an attentional bias (Mather and Carstensen, 2003; Isaacowitz et al., 2008; Brassen et al., 2011; Brassen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mather and Carstensen, 2003; Isaacowitz et al., 2008; Brassen et al., 2011; and Brassen et al., 2012.

claim: Studies involving cognitive manipulation tend to support the relevance of cognitive resources in promoting top-down regulation.
source: Studies involving cognitive manipulation tend to support the relevance of cognitive resources in promoting top-down regulation (Kryla-Lighthall and Mather, 2009; Brassen et al., 2011; Brassen et al., 2012; Mather, 2012; Sasse et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kryla-Lighthall and Mather, 2009; Brassen et al., 2011; Brassen et al., 2012; Mather, 2012; and Sasse et al., 2014.

claim: An attentional positivity effect in older adults during an emotional interference task occurred only when more attentional resources were available.
source: For example, an attentional PE in older adults during an emotional interference task occurred only when more attentional resources were available (Brassen et al., 2011), and focusing on positive and ignoring negative information was directly related to executive control function in a nonemotional visual search task in older participants (Sasse et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brassen et al., 2011.

claim: Focusing on positive and ignoring negative information was directly related to executive control function in a nonemotional visual search task in older participants.
source: For example, an attentional PE in older adults during an emotional interference task occurred only when more attentional resources were available (Brassen et al., 2011), and focusing on positive and ignoring negative information was directly related to executive control function in a nonemotional visual search task in older participants (Sasse et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sasse et al., 2014.

claim: Studies on early processes and habituation suggest that bottom-up processes are also involved in the emergence of emotional selectivity in older persons.
source: On the other hand, studies on early processes and habituation suggest that bottom-up processes are also involved in the emergence of emotional selectivity in older persons (Gronchi et al., 2018; Petro et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gronchi et al., 2018 and Petro et al., 2021.

claim: Both implicit and explicit processes orchestrate age-related adaptation of emotional behavior as a function of neurocognitive resources, compensatory abilities, and lifelong learning.
source: Most likely, both implicit and explicit processes orchestrate age-related adaptation of emotional behavior as a function of neurocognitive resources, compensatory abilities, and lifelong learning.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the evidence on implicit and explicit processes in emotion regulation.

claim: The selection and pursuit of goals is thought to rely on habitual and flexible control.
source: The selection and pursuit of goals is thought to rely on habitual and flexible control (Cushman and Morris, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cushman and Morris, 2015.

claim: An individual habitually seeks to avoid negative situations and approach positive ones through habitual control.
source: Applied to an emotional context, this could mean that an individual habitually seeks to avoid negative situations and approach positive ones (habitual control), but needs to employ a range of flexible (cognitively controlled), complex strategies (e.g. distract from an emotional stimulus or engage in reappraisal) to achieve this goal, depending on the specific situation and one's resources (Raio et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the application of habitual and flexible control to an emotional context, supported by a citation to Raio et al., 2016.

claim: Implicit processes can be involved in all stages of emotion regulation, from goal selection over monitoring to regulation selection and enactment.
source: Nevertheless, implicit processes can be involved in all stages of emotion regulation, from goal selection over monitoring to regulation selection and enactment (Koole et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Koole et al., 2015.

claim: The goal to prioritize emotional well-being and meaning may first be consciously adopted but later be implicitly activated as a form of stimulus-response pairing by an emotionally relevant context or cue.
source: For instance, the goal to prioritize emotional well-being and meaning may first be consciously adopted but later be implicitly activated as a form of stimulus-response pairing by an emotionally relevant context or cue (Williams et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Williams et al., 2009.

claim: Monitoring divergences of emotional responses from goals may occur on implicit levels and has been related to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex/ventral anterior cingulate cortex.
source: Whether or not to engage in emotion regulation is then determined by monitoring divergences of emotional responses from this goal, that, at least in part, may also occur on implicit levels and has been related to the vmPFC/ventral ACC (Etkin et al., 2006; Etkin et al., 2015; Egner et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Etkin et al., 2006; Etkin et al., 2015; and Egner et al., 2008.

claim: Habitual strategies, formed by frequent and consistent use and linked to certain situations, can be elicited automatically when dealing with undesired emotions.
source: Specifically, habitual strategies, formed by frequent and consistent use and linked to certain situations (if-then implementations), can be elicited automatically when dealing with undesired emotions (Christou-Champi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Christou-Champi et al., 2015.

claim: Implicit emotion regulation may bias attention toward stimuli that may help to achieve goals.
source: Such implicit emotion regulation may also bias attention toward stimuli that may help to achieve goals (Vogt et al., 2011), which is particularly interesting given the frequent finding of an attentional positivity bias observed in emotionally health older adults (Brassen et al., 2011; Reed et al., 2014; Sasse et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vogt et al., 2011; Brassen et al., 2011; Reed et al., 2014; and Sasse et al., 2014.

claim: Implicit regulation has been consistently associated with activation in the ventral/rostral anterior cingulate cortex and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex.
source: On the neural level, implicit regulation has been consistently associated with activation in the ventral/rostral ACC and the vmPFC (Quirk et al., 2006; Egner et al., 2008; Brassen et al., 2011; Etkin et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Quirk et al., 2006; Egner et al., 2008; Brassen et al., 2011; and Etkin et al., 2015.

claim: Implicit regulation may be cognitively less demanding but at the cost of behavioral flexibility.
source: Implicit regulation may be cognitively less demanding but at the cost of behavioral flexibility.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the trade-off between cognitive demand and flexibility.

claim: Cognitive flexibility is a major component of cognitive control, and implicates different prefrontal cortex regions, including the lateral prefrontal cortex and orbitofrontal cortex.
source: Cognitive flexibility is a major component of cognitive control, and implicates different PFC regions, including the lateral PFC and orbitofrontal cortex (Friedman and Robbins, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Friedman and Robbins, 2022.

claim: The choice of explicit, goal-directed emotion regulation depends heavily on the individual's ability to weigh the costs and benefits of applying or refraining from control.
source: The choice of explicit, goal-directed emotion regulation depends heavily on the individual's ability to weigh the costs and benefits of applying or refraining from control.
evidence: The claim is stated as a principle of emotion regulation.

claim: Engaging in cognitively costly strategies occurs when the expected benefits of doing so outweigh the costs.
source: In other words, engaging in cognitively costly strategies (e.g. reappraisal, Buhle et al., 2014) occurs when the expected benefits of doing so outweigh the costs (Kool et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Buhle et al., 2014 and Kool et al., 2018.

claim: The capacity for both cost-benefit analysis and cognitively demanding explicit strategies mainly relies on prefrontal function, with the dorso- and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex playing a particular role.
source: The capacity for both cost-benefit analysis and cognitively demanding explicit strategies mainly relies on prefrontal function, with the dorso- and ventrolateral PFC playing a particular role (Smittenaar et al., 2013; Buhle et al., 2014; Cortese, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Smittenaar et al., 2013; Buhle et al., 2014; and Cortese, 2022.

claim: How and when people engage in cost-benefit trade-offs change across the lifespan.
source: Given pronounced age-related changes in the (dorso)lateral PFC (Fjell et al., 2009; Cabeza and Dennis, 2013), it seems likely that how and when people engage in such cost-benefit trade-offs change across the lifespan.
evidence: The claim is inferred from age-related changes in the dorsolateral PFC, supported by citations to Fjell et al., 2009 and Cabeza and Dennis, 2013.

claim: Older adults show an increase in subjectively perceived cognitive costs, which reduces their motivation to engage in cognitively demanding activities.
source: Indeed, older adults show an increase in subjectively perceived cognitive costs, which reduces their motivation to engage in cognitively demanding activities (Hess et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hess et al., 2016.

claim: When motivation is high and task requirements are manageable, older individuals are still able to selectively invest cognitive resources in cognitively costly decision-making.
source: Interestingly, recent lifespan data suggest that when motivation is high and task requirements are manageable, older individuals are still able to selectively invest cognitive resources in cognitively costly decision-making (Devine et al., 2021; Ruel et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Devine et al., 2021 and Ruel et al., 2021.

claim: Neurobehavioral findings in successful aging suggest that there may be a shift in the balance from flexible to implicit habitual control in the second half of life.
source: Overall, neurobehavioral findings in successful aging suggest that there may be a shift in the balance from flexible to implicit habitual control in the second half of life.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the neurobehavioral findings discussed in the preceding sections.

claim: Adaptation in self-control is clearly a lifelong process but probably particularly critical in midlife.
source: Adaptation in self-control is clearly a lifelong process but probably particularly critical in midlife, not only because it is a phase of fundamental internal and external changes but also because individuals are still capable to build aging preparedness (Lachman et al., 2015; Richmond-Rakerd et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the importance of midlife changes and aging preparedness, supported by citations to Lachman et al., 2015 and Richmond-Rakerd et al., 2021.

claim: Large cross-sectional epidemiological surveys consistently show a U-shaped pattern of subjective well-being with an average nadir around age 50.
source: Large cross-sectional epidemiological surveys can provide a detailed look at emotional trajectories and potentially critical time windows for adaptation across the lifespan. They consistently show a U-shaped pattern of subjective well-being with an average nadir around age 50.
evidence: The claim is stated as a consistent finding from epidemiological surveys.

claim: The midlife nadir corresponds to the peak of unhappiness in the late 40s across Europe and the United States.
source: This midlife nadir corresponds to the peak of unhappiness in the late 40s across Europe and the United States (Blanchflower, 2020; Blanchflower, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blanchflower, 2020 and Blanchflower, 2021.

claim: The U-shape in well-being has been observed in more than 140 developing and developed countries.
source: The U-shape has been observed in more than 140 developing and developed countries and holds regardless of whether sociodemographic covariates or cohort effects are included (Blanchflower and Oswald, 2008; Stone et al., 2010; Blanchflower, 2021; Kaiser et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blanchflower and Oswald, 2008; Stone et al., 2010; Blanchflower, 2021; and Kaiser et al., 2022.

claim: The U-shape in well-being holds regardless of whether sociodemographic covariates or cohort effects are included.
source: The U-shape has been observed in more than 140 developing and developed countries and holds regardless of whether sociodemographic covariates or cohort effects are included (Blanchflower and Oswald, 2008; Stone et al., 2010; Blanchflower, 2021; Kaiser et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blanchflower and Oswald, 2008; Stone et al., 2010; Blanchflower, 2021; and Kaiser et al., 2022.

claim: Midlife is considered a critical period for preparing for the demands of aging.
source: Although midlife is considered a critical period for preparing for the demands of aging (Richmond-Rakerd et al., 2021), compared with earlier and later life stages, the factors that mediate well-being in the middle years are less well understood (Lachman et al., 2015), nor is it known whether a potential low point is predictive of later mood.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Richmond-Rakerd et al., 2021.

claim: The factors that mediate well-being in the middle years are less well understood compared with earlier and later life stages.
source: Although midlife is considered a critical period for preparing for the demands of aging (Richmond-Rakerd et al., 2021), compared with earlier and later life stages, the factors that mediate well-being in the middle years are less well understood (Lachman et al., 2015), nor is it known whether a potential low point is predictive of later mood.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lachman et al., 2015.

claim: It is not known whether a potential low point in midlife is predictive of later mood.
source: Although midlife is considered a critical period for preparing for the demands of aging (Richmond-Rakerd et al., 2021), compared with earlier and later life stages, the factors that mediate well-being in the middle years are less well understood (Lachman et al., 2015), nor is it known whether a potential low point is predictive of later mood.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: Mediators of well-being at midlife include the approaching of physical, cognitive, and socioeconomic demands as well as age discrimination by employers, financial pressures, limited opportunities, and changing family dynamics.
source: Mediators of well-being at midlife that have been discussed include the approaching of physical, cognitive, and socioeconomic demands as well as age discrimination by employers, financial pressures, limited opportunities, and changing family dynamics such as parental caregiving and empty-nest transitions (although children leaving home has also been discussed as a later positive factor for well-being because of lower levels of family conflict and financial burden; Stone et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stone et al., 2010.

claim: White matter integrity of prefrontal-subcortical connections starts to degenerate significantly between 40 and 50 years of age.
source: Specifically, white matter integrity of prefrontal-subcortical connections starts to degenerate significantly between 40 and 50 years of age (Gunning-Dixon et al., 2009; Yeatman et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gunning-Dixon et al., 2009 and Yeatman et al., 2014.

claim: White matter decline may be further accelerated by white matter lesions, which first peak in the mid-40s.
source: White matter decline may be further accelerated by WMLs, which first peak in the mid-40s (Moura et al., 2019) and which are then already associated with cognitive decline (d'Arbeloff et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Moura et al., 2019 and d'Arbeloff et al., 2019.

claim: White matter lesions in the mid-40s are already associated with cognitive decline.
source: White matter decline may be further accelerated by WMLs, which first peak in the mid-40s (Moura et al., 2019) and which are then already associated with cognitive decline (d'Arbeloff et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to d'Arbeloff et al., 2019.

claim: Pronounced occurrence of white matter lesions may be driven by an increase of cardiovascular dysfunctions or inflammatory processes associated with metabolic diseases such as obesity, which become more prevalent during midlife.
source: Pronounced occurrence of WMLs may be driven by an increase of cardiovascular dysfunctions or inflammatory processes associated with metabolic diseases such as obesity, which also become more prevalent during midlife (Power et al., 2017; Mattson and Arumugam, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Power et al., 2017 and Mattson and Arumugam, 2018.

claim: Gray matter changes have been related to cognitive decline, particularly in executive functions.
source: Similarly, gray matter changes have been related to cognitive decline, particularly in executive functions (Ferreira et al., 2014; Park and Festini, 2016), which can be observed as early as age 40 (Singh-Manoux et al., 2012; Ferguson et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ferreira et al., 2014 and Park and Festini, 2016.

claim: Cognitive decline in executive functions can be observed as early as age 40.
source: Similarly, gray matter changes have been related to cognitive decline, particularly in executive functions (Ferreira et al., 2014; Park and Festini, 2016), which can be observed as early as age 40 (Singh-Manoux et al., 2012; Ferguson et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Singh-Manoux et al., 2012 and Ferguson et al., 2021.

claim: Cognitive abilities are most important for successful adaptation.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cañas et al., 2003.

claim: Deficits in cognitive control are related to the use of maladaptive emotion-regulation strategies.

claim: Deficits in cognitive control increase individuals' vulnerability for the first onset of depression.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gotlib and Joormann, 2010.

claim: Cognitive capacity is relevant for the successful use of cognitively demanding strategies.

claim: Cognitive capacity is relevant for the flexible selection of adequate strategies in light of changing resources.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Urry and Gross, 2010 and Heckhausen et al., 2019.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Heckhausen et al., 2019.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kiesow et al., 2021.

claim: The increasing awareness of the aging mind and body, limited opportunities, and decreasing time horizon may be particularly crucial for well-being as people in middle age tend to review their 'first half' of life.

claim: Negative mood, negative attitudes toward aging, affective instability, chronic stress, as well as less optimism in nondepressed midlife adults predict later depression.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dennerstein et al., 2004; Lachman et al., 2015; and Campbell et al., 2020.
